No voxel grids or large feature volumes are stored [S4].

The evidence explicitly states that the proposed method represents the scene as a Neural Light Field (NeLF) using a single deep residual MLP network. It contrasts this with methods like KiloNeRF (which uses thousands of small networks) and NeRF (which requires ray-marching and iterative sampling). The text emphasizes that the method avoids ray-marching and uses a single forward pass per ray, implying that no voxel grids or large feature volumes (typical of grid-based or large-volume NeRF representations) are stored or required for the inference process. The representation is compactly stored within the weights of the single deep MLP.

The method takes a camera ray, represented as a concatenation of the spatial coordinates of $K$ sampled points along the ray, forming a $3K$-dimensional input vector [S4].

The evidence explicitly states that the Neural Light Field (NeLF) method maps a '4D oriented ray' (defined by origin and direction) directly to RGB values, thereby 'avoiding the need of sampling multiple points along the camera ray' and 'bypassing the ray-marching and alpha-composition steps'. The claim that the input is a 'concatenation of the spatial coordinates of K sampled points' describes the input format of the original NeRF (which samples points along the ray), not the NeLF method described in the source. The source notes mentioning 'Input vector for NeLF: Concatenation of spatial coordinates of K sampled points' appear to be contradictory artifacts or misinterpretations within the provided text snippets, as the main body and methodology sections consistently define the NeLF input as the 4D ray (origin + direction) and emphasize the elimination of point sampling.
